lessonTitle: Pressure-Volume Events of the Cardiac Cycle

blocks.text: Place a stethoscope on the chest of a healthy teenager and you hear two sounds, a soft 'lub' and a sharper 'dub', repeating about once a second. They are not the sound of muscle contracting; they are the sound of heart valves snapping shut. Each is a landmark on the pressure-volume story of the left ventricle, and together they let you read the cardiac cycle with your ears.

blocks.markdown:
The cardiac cycle is the sequence of pressure and volume changes that occurs in one heartbeat. It is organised around **systole** (ventricular contraction and ejection) and **diastole** (ventricular relaxation and filling). Valves are passive: they open and close purely because of pressure differences across them. A valve opens when the pressure upstream exceeds the pressure downstream, and closes when the pressure gradient reverses.

The left heart has four relevant structures: the left atrium (LA), the mitral valve (the atrioventricular valve between LA and left ventricle), the left ventricle (LV), and the aortic valve (between LV and aorta). We follow LV pressure and volume against these valves. Typical values for a resting healthy adult are an end-diastolic volume (EDV) of about 120 mL, an end-systolic volume (ESV) of about 50 mL, a peak LV pressure of about 120 mmHg and a diastolic aortic pressure of about 80 mmHg; individuals differ.

blocks.title: Key terms
blocks.text: End-diastolic volume (EDV) is the LV volume at the end of filling, when the mitral valve closes. End-systolic volume (ESV) is the LV volume at the end of ejection, when the aortic valve closes. Stroke volume (SV) is the volume ejected per beat, EDV minus ESV. Ejection fraction (EF) is the fraction of EDV ejected. Isovolumetric means pressure changes while volume is constant, because both valves are closed.

blocks.caption: Stroke volume and ejection fraction. Volumes in mL; EF is a percentage (typically in the region of 55 to 70 percent in healthy adults).

blocks.markdown: **Walk through the cycle, starting at end-diastole.** (1) **Atrial systole**: the atrium contracts and tops up ventricular filling. (2) **Isovolumetric contraction**: the ventricle begins to contract, LV pressure rises above LA pressure and the mitral valve **closes**, producing the first heart sound, S1. Now both valves are closed, so volume is constant while pressure climbs steeply. (3) **Ejection**: when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg), the aortic valve **opens** and blood is ejected; LV pressure peaks near 120 mmHg and volume falls from EDV to ESV. (4) As ejection ends and the ventricle relaxes, LV pressure falls below aortic pressure and the aortic valve **closes**, producing the second heart sound, S2. A small notch (the dicrotic notch) appears on the aortic pressure trace. (5) **Isovolumetric relaxation**: both valves are closed, pressure falls steeply at constant volume. (6) When LV pressure falls below LA pressure, the mitral valve **opens** and the ventricle fills rapidly, then slowly, until the next atrial systole.

blocks.caption: Phases of the left ventricular cycle.
rows: Rises to about 120 mmHg then falls

blocks.title: Why the aortic valve does not open at once
blocks.prompt: At the start of systole LV pressure is 8 mmHg and aortic pressure is 80 mmHg. After the mitral valve closes, how does the ventricle reach the pressure needed to eject, and what happens to volume meanwhile?

steps.text: The mitral valve closes as soon as LV pressure exceeds LA pressure. LV pressure (8 mmHg) is still far below aortic pressure (80 mmHg), so the aortic valve remains closed.
Both valves are closed, so no blood can enter or leave: LV volume is constant (at EDV).
Continued contraction of an enclosed fixed volume of blood makes LV pressure rise steeply, from 8 mmHg to just above 80 mmHg.
At the instant LV pressure exceeds 80 mmHg the pressure gradient opens the aortic valve and ejection begins.

blocks.answer: Isovolumetric contraction: pressure rises at constant volume until LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure (80 mmHg), at which point the aortic valve opens.

blocks.markdown:
**Heart sounds.** The first heart sound (S1, 'lub') is produced by closure of the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) at the start of ventricular systole. The second heart sound (S2, 'dub') is produced by closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of ventricular ejection, at the start of isovolumetric relaxation. The sounds come from the vibration of the closed valve leaflets, the blood and the walls as the valves snap shut; they are not caused by valve opening. The interval from S1 to S2 is systole; the interval from S2 to the next S1 is diastole.

**The pressure-volume loop.** If you plot LV pressure (vertical axis) against LV volume (horizontal axis) through one cycle, you get a roughly rectangular loop traversed anticlockwise. The bottom edge is filling, with the lower right corner at mitral valve closure (EDV). The right edge is isovolumetric contraction, going up. The top edge is ejection, moving left as volume falls, between aortic valve opening at the top right corner and aortic valve closure at the top left corner (ESV). The left edge is isovolumetric relaxation, going down to the lower left corner, where the mitral valve opens. The **width** of the loop is the stroke volume, and its area is the external work done by the ventricle per beat.

blocks.title: Reading stroke volume and ejection fraction from a loop
blocks.prompt: On an LV pressure-volume loop the mitral valve closes at a volume of 130 mL, and the aortic valve closes at a volume of 55 mL. Find SV and EF.

steps.text: Mitral valve closure is the end-diastolic volume: EDV = 130 mL.
Aortic valve closure is the end-systolic volume: ESV = 55 mL.
SV = EDV - ESV = 130 - 55 = 75 mL (the width of the loop).
EF = SV / EDV = 75 / 130 = 0.577, or about 58 percent.

blocks.answer: SV is 75 mL and EF is about 58 percent, within the typical healthy range.

items: Mitral valve closes: lower right corner, volume equals EDV, S1.
Isovolumetric contraction: vertical rise on the right, both valves closed.
Aortic valve opens: upper right corner when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure.
Ejection: top edge moves left as volume falls from EDV to ESV.
Aortic valve closes: upper left corner at ESV, S2.
Isovolumetric relaxation: vertical fall on the left, then mitral valve opens at the lower left corner and filling begins.

blocks.title: Valves follow pressure, sounds follow closure
blocks.text: Valves open and close only according to pressure gradients, and the heart sounds come from valve closure. S1 marks the start of isovolumetric contraction (AV valves close) and S2 marks the start of isovolumetric relaxation (semilunar valves close). Volume changes only during filling and ejection.

blocks.title: Loop width is the stroke volume
blocks.text: The horizontal width of the loop is SV. Do not read stroke volume off the pressure axis. A loop that is narrow has a small SV; the labelled corners give EDV and ESV.

points: The cardiac cycle alternates between systole (contraction and ejection) and diastole (relaxation and filling), with valves operating passively on pressure gradients.
The LV cycle consists of isovolumetric contraction, ejection, isovolumetric relaxation and filling; volume is constant during the two isovolumetric phases.
S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves; S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves.
On a pressure-volume loop, the width equals stroke volume (EDV minus ESV), and EF = SV / EDV.

questions.stem: At which moment does the aortic valve open during the cardiac cycle?

options.text: When left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure
When left atrial pressure rises above left ventricular pressure
When left ventricular volume reaches its minimum
When the second heart sound is heard

questions.correctOptionText: When left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the valve opens when the ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, which ends isovolumetric contraction.
distractorRationale.b: This pressure relationship opens the mitral valve, not the aortic valve.
distractorRationale.c: Minimum LV volume (ESV) occurs at the end of ejection, when the aortic valve closes.
distractorRationale.d: S2 is produced by aortic valve closure, not opening.

questions.explanation: Valves are passive and respond to pressure gradients. The aortic valve opens at the end of isovolumetric contraction, when the rising LV pressure first exceeds the aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg diastolic), and blood is ejected.

questions.stem: True or false: During isovolumetric contraction the left ventricular volume stays constant while the pressure rises steeply.
questions.explanation: Both the mitral and aortic valves are closed during isovolumetric contraction, so no blood enters or leaves the ventricle. Contraction of the enclosed fixed volume therefore raises pressure at constant volume.

questions.stem: A student listens to a normal heart. The first heart sound (S1) is caused by which event?

options.text: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of ejection
Opening of the mitral valve at the start of diastole
Opening of the aortic valve at the start of ejection

questions.correctOptionText: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole

distractorRationale.a: Correct: S1 is produced by closure of the atrioventricular valves as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure.
distractorRationale.b: This produces the second heart sound (S2).
distractorRationale.d: Normal aortic valve opening is silent in a healthy heart.

questions.explanation: S1 is the sound of the mitral and tricuspid valves closing at the start of ventricular systole, when ventricular pressure first exceeds atrial pressure. It marks the start of isovolumetric contraction, and it is a closing sound, not an opening sound.

questions.stem: The second heart sound (S2) coincides with which event on the left ventricular pressure and volume traces?

options.text: Aortic valve closure at the end of ejection, as isovolumetric relaxation begins
Peak left ventricular pressure during ejection
Mitral valve opening as filling begins

questions.correctOptionText: Aortic valve closure at the end of ejection, as isovolumetric relaxation begins

distractorRationale.a: Correct: S2 marks closure of the semilunar valves and the start of isovolumetric relaxation at ESV.
distractorRationale.c: Peak LV pressure occurs mid-ejection with the aortic valve open, so no valve sound occurs.
distractorRationale.d: Mitral opening is normally silent and follows isovolumetric relaxation.

questions.explanation: S2 is generated when the aortic (and pulmonary) valves close as LV pressure falls below aortic pressure at the end of ejection. At that moment LV volume is at its minimum (ESV) and isovolumetric relaxation begins.

questions.stem: On a left ventricular pressure-volume loop, which feature gives the stroke volume?

options.text: The horizontal width of the loop, from the volume at aortic valve closure to the volume at mitral valve closure
The peak pressure on the vertical axis
The vertical height between mitral valve opening and aortic valve closure
The volume at the lower left corner of the loop alone

questions.correctOptionText: The horizontal width of the loop, from the volume at aortic valve closure to the volume at mitral valve closure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: SV is EDV minus ESV, which is the width of the loop.
distractorRationale.b: Peak pressure reflects ventricular and afterload conditions, not volume ejected.
distractorRationale.c: Height is a pressure difference, not a volume.
distractorRationale.d: This volume is the ESV, a single end-point rather than the volume ejected.

questions.explanation: The loop's right edge sits at EDV (mitral closure) and its left edge at ESV (aortic closure). The width between them, EDV minus ESV, is the volume ejected per beat, the stroke volume.

questions.stem: A left ventricular pressure-volume loop shows the mitral valve closing at 140 mL and the aortic valve closing at 60 mL. Calculate the stroke volume in mL.
questions.explanation: Mitral closure marks the end-diastolic volume (140 mL) and aortic closure marks the end-systolic volume (60 mL). SV = 140 - 60 = 80 mL, which is the width of the loop.

questions.stem: A patient has end-diastolic volume 150 mL and end-systolic volume 100 mL on a pressure-volume loop. Calculate the ejection fraction as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Stroke volume is 150 - 100 = 50 mL, and EF = 50 / 150 = 0.333, or 33 percent. This is well below the typical healthy range of roughly 55 to 70 percent and indicates the ventricle ejects a reduced fraction of its filling volume, with a narrow loop and high end-systolic volume.

questions.stem: Describe the changes in left ventricular pressure and volume, and the state of the mitral and aortic valves, in each phase of the cardiac cycle from end-diastole to the end of filling.
markingGuide: Isovolumetric contraction: mitral closes, aortic still closed, pressure rises steeply, volume constant at EDV
Ejection: aortic opens when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure; pressure peaks (about 120 mmHg) and volume falls to ESV
Isovolumetric relaxation: aortic closes when LV pressure falls below aortic pressure; both valves closed; pressure falls at constant volume
Filling: mitral opens when LV pressure falls below LA pressure; volume rises rapidly then slowly, with atrial systole at the end
States valves open and close passively with pressure gradients
questions.explanation: The cycle consists of isovolumetric contraction (volume constant, pressure rising), ejection (aortic valve open, volume falling), isovolumetric relaxation (both valves closed, pressure falling) and filling (mitral valve open, volume rising). The valves follow pressure gradients, and the transitions occur when LV pressure crosses LA or aortic pressure.

questions.stem: Explain what produces the first and second heart sounds and where each falls in the cardiac cycle.
markingGuide: S1 is caused by closure of the mitral and tricuspid (atrioventricular) valves
S1 occurs at the start of ventricular systole, at the start of isovolumetric contraction
S2 is caused by closure of the aortic and pulmonary (semilunar) valves
S2 occurs at the end of ejection, at the start of isovolumetric relaxation
The sounds are from valve closure and vibration of blood and walls, not from valve opening; S1 to S2 is systole
questions.explanation: S1 comes from closure of the AV valves as the ventricle starts to contract, and S2 from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves as ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure. These are closing sounds, and together they mark the boundaries of systole.

questions.stem: A left ventricular pressure-volume loop has its lower right corner at 125 mL, upper left corner at 55 mL and peak pressure of about 120 mmHg. Identify what happens at each corner of the loop and each side, and calculate the stroke volume and ejection fraction.
markingGuide: Lower right corner (125 mL): mitral valve closes, EDV; S1
Right side going up: isovolumetric contraction at constant volume
Upper right corner: aortic valve opens when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure; top edge is ejection with volume falling
Upper left corner (55 mL): aortic valve closes, ESV; S2
Left side going down: isovolumetric relaxation; lower left corner mitral valve opens and filling begins
SV = 125 - 55 = 70 mL, the width of the loop
questions.explanation: Mitral closure at 125 mL marks EDV and aortic closure at 55 mL marks ESV, so SV = 125 - 55 = 70 mL, the loop width. EF = 70 / 125 = 0.56 or 56 percent. The vertical sides are the isovolumetric phases, the top edge is ejection and the bottom edge is filling.
